lateinamerika#sections.3.paragraphs.1: For a long time Spain allowed trade with its colonies only through Seville and later Cádiz; as a rule, armed fleets sailed every year to Veracruz and to the coasts of Panama and Colombia. Via the Manila galleon Mexican silver reached Asia, where it was exchanged for silk and porcelain. Smuggling with the English, French and Dutch flourished nonetheless, and the colonies developed their own markets for food, textiles and livestock.
lateinamerika#sections.3.paragraphs.2: Brazil and the Caribbean became centres of sugar production: on plantations with sugar mills, enslaved people processed the cane under murderous conditions into raw sugar for Europe. Around 1700 a gold rush in Minas Gerais set off a wave of migration in Brazil. After independence the countries opened up to world trade and exported coffee, guano, nitrate, wheat, beef and rubber; railways, ports and telegraphs were mostly built with British and later also US capital. This export-oriented economy brought growth but made the countries dependent on fluctuating world market prices.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#summary: Between the Thirty Years' War and the French Revolution, kings rule with a claim to absolute power, while natural science and the Enlightenment spread reason, freedom, and criticism of church and crown.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#overview.0: The 17th century began with a catastrophe: between 1618 and 1648 the Thirty Years' War devastated large parts of Central Europe. What began as a conflict between Catholic and Protestant estates in the Holy Roman Empire became a European struggle for power, into which Denmark, Sweden, Spain, and France intervened. The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 ended the war, confirmed the equal standing of the confessions, and strengthened the territorial rulers against the emperor.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#overview.1: Out of the experience of war and chaos absolutism grew: the king was to rule alone and without restriction, supported by a standing army, officials, and a directed economy. Louis XIV of France, the Sun King, made Versailles the model for the courts of Europe. Peter the Great forced Russia to modernize and founded St Petersburg as a window to the West. In England, by contrast, Parliament imposed limits on royal power in the Glorious Revolution of 1688.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#overview.2: At the same time the new natural science changed the way people thought. Galileo, Kepler, and Isaac Newton described nature with mathematical laws; Newton's Principia of 1687 explained the motion of the planets and the fall of an apple by the same principles. Academies, specialist journals, and experiments took the place of the old authorities. These successes encouraged people to examine the state, law, and religion by reason as well.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#overview.3: The Enlightenment of the 18th century put everything to the test. Voltaire fought against fanaticism and censorship, Montesquieu called for the separation of powers, Rousseau devised a state based on the sovereignty of the people, and the Encyclopédie of Diderot and d'Alembert collected the knowledge of the age. Kant summed up the programme in the statement that enlightenment is man's emergence from his self-imposed immaturity. Rulers such as Frederick II of Prussia called themselves enlightened, but held fast to their absolute power.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#overview.4: Outside Europe, China under the Qing dynasty reached its greatest extent, while in North America English, French, and Spanish colonies grew. The Seven Years' War from 1756 to 1763 was fought out on three continents and made Great Britain the leading colonial power. On the eve of the French Revolution the Enlightenment had undermined the legitimacy of the old order, and with the steam engine a new age was already announcing itself.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#consequences.0: The Peace of Westphalia established a European system of sovereign states that forms the basis of international relations to this day.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#consequences.1: The absolutist state created standing armies, bodies of officials, and central administrations, out of which the modern states emerged.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#consequences.2: The scientific revolution established experiment, observation, and mathematics as the basis of knowledge and made the technology of industrialization possible.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#consequences.3: The ideas of the Enlightenment, such as human rights, the separation of powers, popular sovereignty, and tolerance, became the programme of the American and the French Revolution.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#consequences.4: English parliamentary rule after 1688 became the model for constitutional monarchies and parliamentary systems throughout the world.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#keyFacts.0: From 1618 to 1648 the Thirty Years' War devastates Central Europe; the Peace of Westphalia establishes the system of sovereign states.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#keyFacts.1: In 1633 Galileo has to abjure the heliocentric world view before the Inquisition; in 1687 Newton describes gravitation mathematically.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#keyFacts.2: In 1649 the English Parliament has King Charles I executed; in 1689 the Bill of Rights secures the rights of Parliament permanently.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#keyFacts.3: In 1683 the second Ottoman siege of Vienna fails; Austria rises to become a great power in south-eastern Europe.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#keyFacts.4: Louis XIV rules France for 72 years, makes Versailles the model for Europe, and drives out the Huguenots in 1685.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#keyFacts.5: In 1748 Montesquieu calls for the separation of powers, in 1762 Rousseau devises the social contract, and in 1784 Kant defines enlightenment.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#keyFacts.6: From 1639 Japan closes itself off almost completely from the outside world, while James Cook charts the Pacific between 1768 and 1779.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#sections.0.para: The absolutist state rested on three pillars: a standing army that the king maintained even in peacetime, a paid body of officials that pushed the nobility out of the administration, and a directed economy that provided the money for both. In France, Richelieu and Mazarin imposed this order against the resistance of the nobility, which Louis XIV finally bound to the court after the revolt of the Fronde. The king was held to be appointed by God, and Bishop Bossuet taught that no one might demand an account from him. In practice provincial estates, parlements, and privileges continued to exist, and royal power was never as unrestricted as the theory claimed.

England took a different path. The conflict between king and Parliament over taxes and religion led in 1642 to the civil war, which ended with the execution of Charles I and the republic under Oliver Cromwell. After the return of the monarchy in 1660 and the Glorious Revolution of 1688 it was clear that the king could govern only with Parliament. John Locke supplied the justification: governments exist to protect life, liberty, and property, and may be deposed if they violate this task.

In the 18th century the European system of powers was determined by five great powers: France, Great Britain, Austria, Prussia, and Russia. Wars such as the War of the Spanish Succession, the War of the Austrian Succession, and the Seven Years' War turned on the balance of power, claims of inheritance, and colonies. Rulers such as Frederick II, Maria Theresa, Joseph II, and Catherine II called themselves enlightened and reformed schools, justice, and administration, but in 1772 jointly partitioned Poland and held fast to their unlimited power.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#sections.1.para: Society was divided into estates: the clergy and the nobility enjoyed exemption from taxes and privileges of honour, while the Third Estate, that is peasants, craftsmen, merchants, and scholars, bore the burdens. The Thirty Years' War had depopulated Germany, and only around 1700 was the level of 1618 reached again. Famines, infant mortality, and epidemics determined everyday life; the plague raged in London in 1665 and in Marseille in 1720. The witch trials, which reached their peak between 1560 and 1630, claimed tens of thousands of victims in Europe, predominantly women.

At the same time a new public sphere emerged. In coffee houses, reading societies, salons, and Masonic lodges, townspeople and nobles discussed politics, science, and literature. Newspapers and journals such as the English Spectator reached a growing readership, and the number of people able to read rose. Women such as the Marquise du Deffand or Madame Geoffrin ran salons in Paris where the thinkers of the Enlightenment met, and scholars such as Émilie du Châtelet or the astronomer Maria Winkelmann carried out research despite all obstacles.

At court, ceremonial governed every step. The king's rising and dressing was a public act at Versailles, in which the order of those present showed their rank. Wigs, hooped skirts, chocolate, and coffee spread from the court into the cities. For the majority of people in the countryside, however, little changed; in Eastern Europe serfdom even grew harsher, and in Russia landowners could sell their peasants like cattle.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#sections.2.para: The scientific revolution changed the relationship of human beings to the world. In 1609 Galileo turned the telescope on the heavens, Kepler found the laws of the planetary orbits, William Harvey discovered the circulation of the blood, and Newton brought heaven and earth together under a single law. Academies such as the Royal Society in London and the Académie des sciences in Paris organized the exchange of observations, experiments, and criticism. The microscope, the telescope, the air pump, and the pendulum clock extended the senses and made measurement the basis of knowledge.

The Enlightenment transferred this confidence in reason to society, law, and religion. Pierre Bayle and Voltaire demanded tolerance, Montesquieu examined the laws and constitutions of peoples, Rousseau asked after a just order, and Beccaria called for the abolition of torture and the death penalty. Deism saw in God a clockmaker who had created the world and no longer intervened in it; others remained devout but demanded a reasonable religion without superstition. In Germany, Lessing, Mendelssohn, and Kant combined the Enlightenment with religious tolerance and ethics.

Art and music flourished with the Baroque and the Rococo. Magnificent palaces, churches and gardens such as those at Versailles, Würzburg and Schönbrunn were meant to display the power of princes and church. Johann Sebastian Bach, George Frideric Handel and later Haydn and Mozart created works that belong to the core of European music. The Lisbon earthquake of 1755 shook the belief in a best of all possible worlds and set off a debate about God, nature and evil that Voltaire took up in his Candide.
absolutismus-aufklaerung#sections.3.para: Mercantilism was the economic doctrine of absolutism. According to Colbert's ideas, a state should export more than it imported in order to keep gold and silver in the country. Manufactories for luxury goods such as tapestries, mirrors and porcelain were founded, tariffs protected domestic production, and colonies supplied raw materials and bought finished goods. In Prussia and Austria the doctrine was called cameralism and served above all to fill the prince's coffers for the army and the administration.

The Netherlands and England developed a different form of economic activity. Trading companies such as the Dutch and the English East India Company were joint-stock companies with their own fleets, fortresses and soldiers; the Amsterdam stock exchange and the Bank of England, founded in 1694, became centers of capital. The triangular trade between Europe, Africa and the Americas in goods, slaves and plantation products such as sugar, tobacco and coffee brought enormous profits. In 1776 Adam Smith criticized mercantilism and called for free trade as the source of prosperity.

In agriculture, the agricultural revolution began in England with new crop rotations, the cultivation of clover, animal breeding and the enclosure of common land. The potato prevailed against resistance in Prussia and other countries and reduced famines. From 1712 onward, steam engines of Newcomen's design pumped water out of mines, and the improvement by James Watt from 1769 as well as mechanical spinning machines announced industrialization. Canals, paved roads and stagecoaches sped up traffic within Europe.
revolutionen#summary: From American independence through the French Revolution and Napoleon to the Revolution of 1848: human rights, nation and popular sovereignty overthrow the old order.
revolutionen#overview.0: In 1776 thirteen British colonies in North America declared their independence, invoking the Enlightenment: all men are created equal and have a right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. Under George Washington and with French help they won the war against the mother country. The Constitution of 1787 created the first modern republic with a separation of powers and an elected president.
revolutionen#overview.1: France had overstretched itself financially by supporting the Americans. When King Louis XVI convened the Estates General in 1789, the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly, and on 14 July the people of Paris stormed the Bastille. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, the abolition of noble privileges and a constitution followed. The attempt to preserve the monarchy failed; in 1792 the republic was proclaimed and in 1793 the king was executed.
revolutionen#overview.2: Threatened by enemies abroad and uprisings at home, the Jacobins under Robespierre established a reign of terror to which thousands of people fell victim on the guillotine. In the colony of Saint-Domingue, too, the enslaved rose up in 1791; under Toussaint Louverture they won the abolition of slavery, and in 1804 Haiti came into being as the first state founded by former slaves. Olympe de Gouges demanded equal rights for women and was executed for it.
revolutionen#overview.3: Out of the revolutionary wars rose the general Napoleon Bonaparte, who seized power in a coup in 1799 and crowned himself emperor in 1804. He reorganized France with the Code civil, defeated Austria, Prussia and Russia and dominated almost all of Europe. The campaign into Russia in 1812 ended in catastrophe; the Battle of the Nations at Leipzig in 1813 and Waterloo in 1815 ended his rule. The Congress of Vienna restored the monarchies and sought to suppress revolutionary ideas.
revolutionen#overview.4: Yet the ideas of liberty, nation and constitution could no longer be pushed back. In Latin America, Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín led the Spanish colonies to independence, Greece broke away from the Ottoman Empire, and in 1830 Paris once again overthrew its king. In 1848 a wave of revolution swept across almost all of Europe; in Frankfurt the first all-German national assembly convened. The revolution failed, but its demands for basic rights and national unity remained on the agenda.
revolutionen#consequences.0: The human and civil rights of 1776 and 1789 became the benchmark for constitutions and basic rights throughout the world.
revolutionen#consequences.1: The idea of popular sovereignty replaced the divine right of kings as the basis of political rule and initiated the transition to constitutional states and democracies.
revolutionen#consequences.2: The Code civil spread equality before the law, freedom of property and the separation of state and church across Europe and shaped numerous legal systems.
revolutionen#consequences.3: The revolutions in Haiti and Latin America largely ended European colonial rule on the American continent and set an example against slavery.
revolutionen#consequences.4: Nationalism and liberalism became the defining political forces of the 19th century and led to new nation-states such as Italy and Germany.
revolutionen#keyFacts.0: In 1787 the United States gives itself the first modern written constitution with a separation of powers in Philadelphia; in 1791 the basic rights of the Bill of Rights follow.
revolutionen#keyFacts.1: In October 1789 the march of thousands of Parisian women to Versailles forces the king to move to Paris; in 1794 the National Convention abolishes slavery in the French colonies.
revolutionen#keyFacts.2: From 1798 to 1801 Napoleon's campaign to Egypt fails militarily but establishes modern Egyptology; in 1804 Haiti becomes independent as the first state founded by former slaves.
revolutionen#keyFacts.3: In 1806 Francis II lays down the crown of the Holy Roman Empire; from 1807 onward the Prussian Reforms modernize the state, the army and education.
revolutionen#keyFacts.4: In 1812 Napoleon loses the greater part of his army in Russia; in 1815 his rule ends for good at Waterloo.
revolutionen#keyFacts.5: From 1810 to 1821 Mexico wins its independence from Spain; in 1830 the July Revolution in Paris overthrows the Bourbons.
revolutionen#keyFacts.6: In 1832 around 30,000 people at the Hambach Festival demand freedom and German unity; the colors black, red and gold become the symbol of the movement.
revolutionen#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
revolutionen#sections.0.paragraphs.0: The revolutions in America and France gave a new answer to the same question: where does the power of the state come from? In place of the king by the grace of God came the people as the bearer of sovereignty, giving themselves a constitution through elected representatives. The American Constitution of 1787 put Montesquieu's separation of powers into practice with Congress, president and Supreme Court; within ten years France tried out a constitutional monarchy, a radical republic, the dictatorship of the Committee of Public Safety and the Directory before Napoleon seized power.
revolutionen#sections.0.paragraphs.1: Napoleon ruled as emperor with plebiscites, a compliant parliament and a tightly organized administration, but with his conquests he exported the law code, equality before the law and the dissolution of the old imperial structures to half of Europe. The reforms in Prussia, Bavaria and Austria were in part responses to this challenge: states that wanted to survive had to turn their subjects into citizens who were willing to fight for the fatherland and to pay taxes.
revolutionen#sections.0.paragraphs.2: After 1815 the monarchs under Metternich's leadership tried to turn back the clock. Censorship, police informers, the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819 and the interventions of the Holy Alliance in Spain and Italy were meant to stifle constitutions and national movements. But Great Britain withdrew from the system, Greece, Belgium and the Latin American states won their independence, and the July Revolution of 1830 showed that kings who broke the constitution could be overthrown. The Vormärz, the period between 1815 and 1848, was a race between repression and a growing desire for freedom.
revolutionen#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
revolutionen#sections.1.paragraphs.0: The revolution put an end to the society of estates. Noble titles, tithes, compulsory labor services and guild constraints were abolished in France between 1789 and 1791, church property was auctioned off and peasants became owners of their land. The new masters were the propertied middle class, lawyers, merchants and officials; the artisans and small traders of the cities, the sansculottes, had driven the revolution forward in the streets but mostly remained excluded from the vote. In Prussia the October Edict of 1807 abolished the hereditary subjection of the peasants, yet many lost their land to the manorial lords when redeeming their obligations.
revolutionen#sections.1.paragraphs.1: Women helped carry the revolution, from the march on Versailles through the political clubs to the women who followed Napoleon to war as sutlers. Olympe de Gouges in France and Mary Wollstonecraft in England demanded equal rights, yet in 1793 the revolution excluded women from politics, and the Code civil placed them under the guardianship of men. Slavery was abolished in the French colonies in 1794, reintroduced by Napoleon in 1802 and eliminated in Haiti by the enslaved themselves; in the United States the constitution entrenched slavery, and in 1807 Britain at first banned only the slave trade.
revolutionen#sections.1.paragraphs.2: War shaped the everyday life of an entire generation. General conscription, introduced in France in 1793, sent millions of young men into the armies; billeting, requisitions, epidemics and the British naval blockade struck the civilian population. At the same time a political public sphere emerged with newspapers, pamphlets, songs and festivals such as the Hambach Festival, and colors, cockades and anthems such as the Marseillaise made politics a matter of feeling.
revolutionen#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
revolutionen#sections.2.paragraphs.0: The revolution intervened deeply in religion. In 1789 France nationalized church property, made priests swear an oath to the constitution and in 1793 attempted to replace Christianity with a cult of reason and a new calendar; in the Concordat of 1801 Napoleon reconciled with the pope but kept the church under state supervision. In Germany the Imperial Recess of 1803 dissolved the ecclesiastical principalities and monasteries, and Jews received civil rights for the first time in France in 1791 and in Prussia in 1812.
revolutionen#sections.2.paragraphs.1: Art became political. Jacques-Louis David painted the Tennis Court Oath and the murdered Marat, Goya recorded the execution of the Madrid insurgents in 1808, and in 1830 Delacroix created Liberty Leading the People. Beethoven struck out the dedication of his Third Symphony to Napoleon when the latter crowned himself emperor; poets such as Byron and Hölderlin were enthusiastic about the freedom of Greece. Romanticism discovered folk songs, fairy tales and the medieval past and thereby contributed to the emergence of national identities.
revolutionen#sections.2.paragraphs.2: Science and education became tasks of the state. France introduced the metric system, the Polytechnic School and a centrally directed school system; the scholars who accompanied Napoleon to Egypt founded Egyptology with the Description de l'Égypte and the Rosetta Stone. In 1810 Wilhelm von Humboldt founded the University of Berlin on the principle of the unity of research and teaching, and the Brothers Grimm, linguists and historians, made the universities carriers of the national idea.
revolutionen#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
revolutionen#sections.3.paragraphs.0: The revolution created the legal foundations of the market economy: freedom of trade, the abolition of the guilds, protection of property, uniform weights and measures and, in France in 1800, the Bank of France. The Code civil and the Prussian Reforms made it possible to buy and sell land freely and to practice any trade. The customs barriers between hundreds of small German states fell only gradually; the German Customs Union of 1834 was a late fruit of this development.
revolutionen#sections.3.paragraphs.1: Napoleon's Continental Blockade against British goods from 1806 was intended to bring Great Britain economically to its knees, but above all it encouraged smuggling and drove up the prices of sugar and coffee; at the same time it stimulated the cultivation of sugar beet and the textile industry on the continent. Great Britain, protected by its fleet, financed the coalitions against France with the profits of its incipient industrialization and emerged from the wars as the leading economic power.
revolutionen#sections.3.paragraphs.2: The technology of war and of the state changed. Mass armies needed standardized rifles, tin cans, which Napoleon's government brought forth through a prize competition, and the optical telegraph, which carried messages from Paris to the frontiers within hours. After 1815 the steam engine and the railroad reached the continent; the first German railway ran from Nuremberg to Fürth in 1835, and the labor question, which came onto the agenda in 1848, was already making itself felt in the textile towns.
industrialisierung-imperialismus#summary: The steam engine, the factory and the railroad change work and everyday life, new nation-states emerge, and the European powers divide the world into colonies.
industrialisierung-imperialismus#overvie: From the late 18th century onward, an upheaval began in England that is known as the Industrial Revolution. The steam engine improved by James Watt powered spinning machines, looms, pumps and soon locomotives as well. Work shifted from workshops and farms into factories, and coal and iron became the raw materials of the new age. Cities such as Manchester, Birmingham and later the Ruhr region grew many times over within a few decades.

Industrialization created enormous wealth, but also new social questions. Factory workers, among them many women and children, worked twelve hours a day and more, lived in cramped tenements and had hardly any rights. Out of this experience arose trade unions, cooperatives and political parties. In the Communist Manifesto of 1848, Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels interpreted history as a struggle between classes and called for a society without private ownership of the means of production.

At the same time the nation-state became the guiding model of politics. In Europe, new large states emerged with Italy in 1861 and the German Empire in 1871; in the United States the Civil War from 1861 to 1865 secured the unity of the Union and ended slavery. After the Meiji Restoration of 1868, Japan deliberately opened itself to Western technology and administration and rose within a single generation to become an industrial and military power.

With economic and military superiority grew the claim of the industrial states to colonies, raw materials and markets. Great Britain forced China to open up in the Opium War, the Suez Canal shortened the route to India, and at the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885 the European powers laid down rules for the partition of Africa. The resistance of the colonized was often brutally broken, for example in the genocide of the Herero and Nama in German South West Africa.

Around 1900 technical progress seemed boundless: electricity, the telephone, the automobile, the airplane and Marie Curie's discoveries in physics shaped the sense of life. At the same time the great powers armed, concluded alliances and competed over fleets and colonies. These tensions erupted in 1914 in the First World War.
industrialisierung-imperialismus#consequ: The factory, the machine and fossil energy have shaped the economy and everyday life ever since; today's economic growth as well as climate change have their roots here.
Out of the social question arose the labor movement, social legislation and the political ideas of socialism and communism, which determined the 20th century.
Nation-states such as Germany, Italy, the United States and Japan became the decisive actors in world politics.
The colonial partition of Africa and Asia left behind arbitrary borders, economic dependencies and conflicts whose effects are still felt today.
The rivalry of the imperialist great powers led directly into the First World War.
industrialisierung-imperialismus#keyFact: From about 1780 onward, a completely new form of economic activity emerges in England with the steam engine, the mechanical loom and the factory.
In 1833 the British Empire abolishes slavery, in 1861 Russia abolishes serfdom, and in 1865 slavery ends in the United States.
In 1859 Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species shakes the worldview of many people.
In 1863 the Red Cross is founded in Geneva, and in 1864 the first Geneva Convention follows.
From 1883 to 1889 Bismarck introduces the world's first state social insurance schemes.
In 1893 New Zealand becomes the first country in the world in which women receive the vote at the national level.
Around 1900 the European powers, the United States and Japan control almost the entire earth as colonies or spheres of influence.
industrialisierung-imperialismus#section: The 19th century was the age of constitutions and parliaments, but not of democracy in today's sense. In Great Britain the electoral reforms of 1832, 1867 and 1884 gradually widened the circle of voters, while in Prussia the three-class franchise based on tax payments determined the weight of a vote until 1918. Women remained excluded almost everywhere; only New Zealand granted them the vote in 1893, followed by Australia in 1902 and Finland in 1906. Monarchs such as William I, Franz Joseph and Tsar Alexander II ruled with ministers and officials who were increasingly selected according to merit rather than origin.

The nation-state became the dominant political idea. Italy united between 1859 and 1870 under Cavour and Garibaldi, and Germany in 1871 under Prussian leadership. In the multiethnic empires of the Habsburgs, Ottomans and Romanovs, Czechs, Hungarians, Poles, Serbs and other peoples demanded rights of their own or states of their own. Nationalism combined with compulsory schooling, conscription, monuments and national holidays to form a mass movement that placed loyalty to the state above all other ties.
